summary: Learners aged 12–14 investigate how multiple independent lines of evidence — the fossil record, comparative anatomy (homologous structures), and biogeography — converge to support evolution and common ancestry. The core insight is reading deep structural similarity (e.g. the pentadactyl limb shared by human arm, bat wing, whale flipper and horse leg) as evidence of shared ancestry, distinguished from analogous structures that share only function or surface appearance, and treating evolution's strength as lying in the convergence of several independent clues rather than any single one. A linked theme is distinguishing what we OBSERVE (fossils, bones, distributions) from what we INFER (common ancestry).
misconceptions: Thinking evolution is 'just a theory'/guess, not recognising the multiple independent, converging lines of evidence behind it.
Reading any physical similarity as relatedness — confusing analogous structures (convergent, e.g. bird and insect wings) with homologous ones.
Believing the fossil record should be complete, so gaps disprove evolution, rather than understanding fossilisation is rare and the record is necessarily partial.
Assuming fossils give exact ages by themselves or that all fossils are dinosaurs, misunderstanding what the record actually shows.
Thinking humans evolved from modern monkeys/chimps rather than sharing a common ancestor with them.
Treating evolution as directed 'progress' toward humans, rather than branching descent with modification evidenced by the data.

activities.title: Overlay the shared bone plan across four limbs
steps: Examine four forelimbs side by side — a human arm, a bat's wing, a whale's flipper and a horse's front leg — and first note how differently they look and what different jobs they do (gripping, flying, swimming, running).
Select one bone in the human arm (e.g. the single upper-arm bone) and identify the corresponding bone in each of the other three limbs; repeat for the forearm bones, wrist and finger bones.

Colour-match or label corresponding bones across all four limbs so the shared limb plan (upper-arm bone, paired forearm bones, wrist, digits) becomes visible beneath a wing, a flipper and a leg, noting where bones are reduced or fused (e.g. the horse's ulna is reduced and fused to the radius, and it has one main digit).
State in your own words why one inherited bone plan reshaped for different lives points to a common ancestor.
activities.insight: A bat, a whale, a horse and a human are built on the same underlying limb skeleton reshaped for different functions — a pattern best explained by descent from a shared ancestor.

activities.title: Homologous versus analogous: shared structure versus shared function
steps: Compare a bat's wing with an insect's wing — both used for flying.
Check whether the insect wing contains the same bones as the bat wing (it does not; it shares none of the pentadactyl bones).

Compare a shark and a dolphin: both have streamlined bodies and fins and look very alike, yet the dolphin is a mammal whose flipper contains the pentadactyl limb skeleton (the same cetacean/mammalian plan seen in the whale flipper earlier) while the shark is a fish — their resemblance comes from independently adapting to fast swimming, not from a recent shared ancestor.

Classify the bat-wing/human-arm and dolphin-flipper/human-arm pairings as homologous (same structure and origin, different function) and the bat-wing/insect-wing and shark/dolphin resemblances as analogous (same function or appearance, different origin).
Explain why similar function or surface resemblance alone is not evidence of close relatedness.
activities.insight: Structures can look or work alike for different reasons: homologous structures share an inherited plan (evidence of common ancestry), while analogous structures share only a function or appearance arrived at independently (convergence), so 'looks/works similar' does not mean 'closely related'.

activities.title: Read the rock layers: fossils as evidence of change over time
steps: Examine a stratigraphic column and identify which life forms appear in deeper versus shallower rock layers.

Locate a transitional form (e.g. Archaeopteryx) and describe which of its features it shares with earlier reptile/dinosaur groups (teeth, clawed fingers, bony tail) and which with later birds (feathers, wings).
Explain in your own words how a fossil forms and why fossilisation is rare.
Discuss why the fossil record is necessarily patchy and why gaps are expected rather than a disproof of evolution.
activities.insight: Different life forms in older versus younger strata document change over time, and transitional forms link groups; because fossilisation is rare, the record is expected to be incomplete, and gaps do not disprove evolution.

activities.title: Galapagos finches: geography as evidence
steps: Examine a map linking finch species on different Galapagos islands to their beak shapes.
Trace how finches on isolated islands could diverge from a single mainland ancestor.
Explain why the geographic distribution of related species counts as evidence for evolution rather than an abstract claim.
activities.insight: When related species are distributed across isolated locations with differences matching their conditions (e.g. finch beak shapes matching the foods available in different island habitats), that pattern is evidence of divergence from a common ancestor — biogeography is an independent line of evidence.

activities.title: Converging lines of evidence and distinguishing evidence from inference
steps: Bring together the fossil record, comparative anatomy, biogeography (and DNA) and state what each one independently shows.
Draw or describe how these independent clues all point toward the same conclusion of common ancestry.
For each strand, separate what is OBSERVED (fossils, bones, distributions) from what is INFERRED (common ancestry).
Explain, using the idea of convergence, why evolution is more than 'just a theory' or a guess.
activities.insight: Evolution's strength lies in the convergence of multiple independent lines of evidence; a scientific theory is a well-tested explanation, not a casual guess, and we reason (infer) about the unobservable past from observable clues.

activities.title: In role with Darwin or a palaeontologist (discussion extension)
steps: Interview Darwin or a palaeontologist in role about the Beagle voyage, Galapagos species (Darwin was first struck by the mockingbirds and tortoises; the finches' importance became clear later, after experts studied his specimens), and how fossils and anatomy led to the idea of descent with modification.
Ask what the evidence does and does not show, and respond to the claim that evolution is 'just a theory'.
Weigh which clues are strongest and why, articulating the reasoning from evidence to inference.
activities.insight: Scientific conclusions about the deep past are reasoned inferences from evidence; articulating that reasoning in dialogue makes the move from observation to inference explicit and personal.

activities.title: Consolidation: sort, match and check evidence reasoning
steps: Sort given structures into homologous versus analogous.
Match each line of evidence (fossils, anatomy, biogeography) to the inference it supports.
Answer a question on why island finches are evidence for evolution.
Evaluate a statement claiming the fossil record must be complete and explain why it is mistaken.
activities.insight: Consolidating the categories and evidence–inference links reinforces interpretation of given evidence and can surface residual misconceptions.

checkQuestion: A shark and a dolphin both have streamlined bodies and fins and look very alike. A student says this similarity is strong evidence that they are closely related. A bat's wing and a human arm look quite different and do different jobs. Which pair is the better evidence of a shared ancestor, and why?
checkAnswer: The bat wing and human arm. Although they look different and do different jobs, they share the SAME underlying bone arrangement (the pentadactyl limb) — homologous structures inherited from a common ancestor. The shark and dolphin only LOOK alike because both adapted to fast swimming (convergent/analogous), despite very different ancestry. Deep structural similarity, not surface resemblance, is the evidence for common ancestry.
